Reasoning reinforcement learning replaces a fixed target sequence with a space of possible trajectories. The policy must explore that space; an environment must judge the result; and the training algorithm must learn from sparse, noisy, or exploitable rewards. Long outputs are a consequence of this system, not evidence of reasoning by themselves.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

1. formulate reasoning as policy optimization over token trajectories;
2. explain reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and group-relative updates;
3. design an environment, verifier, and difficulty curriculum as one system;
4. distinguish published evidence from speculation in reasoning-model reports; and
5. test for reward hacking, mode collapse, and inefficient overthinking.

## A trajectory-level objective

For prompt $x$, the policy samples a response $y$ and receives reward $R(x,y)$. A reference policy can constrain the update:

$$
\max_\theta\; \mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}[R(x,y)]
-\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_\theta\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\right).
$$

In mathematics, code, and formal tasks, the reward may come from an answer checker, tests, or a proof verifier. These rewards scale more cheaply than human preference labels, but only measure what their checker can observe.

## Exploration and group-relative optimization

Sparse reward creates a bootstrapping problem: if every sampled trajectory fails, the batch provides little information about which decisions helped. Training recipes therefore combine suitable initial competence, diverse sampling, curriculum, reward normalization, and sometimes a small cold-start set.

[DeepSeekMath](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300) introduces Group Relative Policy Optimization [@shao2024deepseekmath]. Instead of fitting a separate critic, GRPO compares rewards among several outputs for the same prompt. In simplified form, the relative advantage for candidate $i$ is

$$
A_i=\frac{r_i-\operatorname{mean}(r_1,\ldots,r_G)}
{\operatorname{std}(r_1,\ldots,r_G)+\epsilon}.
$$

This removes one large component, not the need for careful rewards, reference control, clipping, or exploration analysis.

## The environment is part of the method

An environment maps the present interaction to the next observation, reward, termination signal, and metadata:

$$
(o_{t+1},r_t,\text{done},m_t)=E(o_t,a_t).
$$

The complete contract includes allowed actions, hidden state, checker version, time and token budgets, malformed-output rules, sandbox boundaries, and termination. A tool exposes an operation; an environment defines consequences; a benchmark specifies the task sample and aggregation protocol.

## Open case studies, careful claims

[DeepSeek-R1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948) [@guo2025deepseekr1] reports a staged recipe involving reinforcement learning, curated cold-start data, supervised data, and distillation. [Kimi k1.5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12599) [@team2025kimi] reports a different long-context RL recipe. These reports are valuable evidence about complete systems, but cross-model comparisons do not isolate one algorithm.

For any reasoning model—open or closed—separate four layers:

| Layer | Defensible evidence |
|---|---|
| capability | versioned evaluation under a declared budget |
| training | methods and ablations reported by the developer |
| mechanism | controlled causal evidence |
| unknown | unreported data, reward details, and infrastructure |

## Reward hacking and overthinking

The policy may exploit an answer parser, write code that passes incomplete tests, imitate verifier preferences, or produce long traces because length correlates with reward. Hold out adversarial tests, mutate checkers, inspect reward–correctness disagreements, and report accuracy against both training and private verifiers.

## Studio: a small RLVR gym

Build a versioned environment for arithmetic programs, unit tests, or symbolic expressions. Sample a group of candidates per prompt, score them with an executable verifier, and run either a small policy update or a clearly labelled rejection-sampling surrogate. Vary task difficulty and record reward, true correctness on hidden tests, output length, diversity, and KL from the starting model.

The deliverable includes the environment contract, trajectory schema, reward-hacking attacks, and a plot showing whether training improved correctness or only learned the public checker.

## What to remember

1. RLVR learns from sampled trajectories and checkable outcomes.
2. The verifier, curriculum, and environment are part of the training algorithm.
3. GRPO changes advantage estimation; it does not make reward design disappear.
4. Long traces are a cost whose marginal value must be measured.
5. A technical report documents a system; causal claims still require controlled ablations.
